strengths: Large-scale, carefully documented pretraining pipeline using exclusively open CT datasets (229,619 series across 8 sources), with detailed preprocessing, filtering, and hardware description that supports reproducibility.

Reasonably well-motivated architectural adaptation to the specific challenges of volumetric CT (token scaling, anisotropy, geometry) via a two-stage local/global ViT design with 3D RoPE and DINOv3-style jittering, and a principled adaptation of SigLIP for many-to-many clinical text supervision.

Broad empirical evaluation spanning three distinct task families (frozen-embedding biomarker classification across 6 datasets and 11 competing foundation models, semantic segmentation across 4 datasets, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on 2 datasets), which is more extensive than most concurrent CT foundation model papers.

Encoder-only segmentation protocol (SEoMT) is a clean way to isolate representation quality from decoder engineering, and the paper is transparent about its limitations (loss of fine detail from 1/4-resolution prediction).

Reasonably honest discussion of limitations (thoracic data skew, weaker abdominal performance, noisy report supervision) and inclusion of failure cases/ablations (e.g., optimizer and crop-size ablations, saliency maps, UMAP visualizations) rather than only favorable results.
Public release of training code and pretraining recipes is promised, which could benefit the community given costly compute requirements.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily integrative rather than fundamental: the core components (DINOv3 SSL, SigLIP alignment, 3D RoPE, EoMT-style segmentation head) are directly adapted from existing 2D/3D methods, with limited new methodological contribution beyond engineering choices (windowing, local/global hierarchy) that are not deeply ablated against simpler alternatives (e.g., no ablation isolating the benefit of the two-stage local/global attention scheme itself, or of omitting the Gram loss, versus single-stage baselines).

Pretraining corpus (229K series) is substantially larger than most compared baselines (e.g., FMCIB ~11K, CT-CLIP ~25K, Merlin ~15K), confounding claims that architectural/algorithmic choices rather than data scale drive the reported gains; no controlled scaling comparison is provided.

The abstract's claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' is not fully supported by the results: it loses to Merlin substantially on Findings-based retrieval (Table 3), loses to nnU-Net ResEnc L on KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD segmentation (Table 1), and does not achieve top performance on 2 of 6 biomarker tasks (Fig. 1/3), making the overall framing somewhat overstated relative to the mixed empirical picture.

Several architectural hyperparameters (embedding dimension 1080, G=36 windows, specific patch sizes) appear to be fixed choices without ablation or justification beyond intuition, limiting insight into which design decisions actually matter.

No code/model link is actually provided in the submission (footnote is empty), and reproducibility relies entirely on a promise of future release, which cannot be independently verified at review time.

Statistical comparison is inconsistent across experiments: confidence intervals are reported for biomarker classification but not for segmentation or retrieval results, making it hard to assess whether reported margins (often <1-2 Dice points or moderate recall differences) are meaningful.

strengths: Comprehensive engineering effort: the paper combines a carefully designed local-global 3D ViT architecture (windowed local attention + global aggregation, 3D RoPE with jittering) with a two-stage DINOv3-style SSL + SigLIP VLA pretraining pipeline, and describes hyperparameters, hardware, and data curation in substantial detail, aiding reproducibility.

The pretraining corpus (229k series from 8 public datasets) is entirely open, and the authors commit to releasing code, which is valuable for the community compared to many closed-data CT foundation models.

Broad and fairly rigorous evaluation across three task families (biomarker classification via frozen kNN, semantic segmentation via encoder-only SEoMT integrated into nnU-Net, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval), with confidence intervals, saliency maps, decoder ablations, and robustness checks (text dropout, spacing robustness) that go beyond a single headline metric.

Reasonable comparisons against many strong baselines (11 CT foundation models for biomarker prediction, several transformer segmentation backbones, CT-CLIP/Merlin/OpenCLIP/BioMedCLIP for retrieval), and honest reporting of cases where SPECTRE does not win (e.g., CT-FM on TotalSegmentator, Merlin on Findings retrieval, NSCLC-Radiogenomics/Colorectal-Liver-Metastases AUC).

The decoder ablation (Linear vs SEoMT vs UNETR) is a self-critical analysis showing the limits of the encoder-only evaluation protocol and clarifying that reported segmentation numbers likely underestimate the encoder's true capability.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'consistently outperforming prior CT foundation models' is only partially supported: SPECTRE wins on 4/6 biomarker tasks (with large CIs on 2 of the 4 losing tasks suggesting weak separation), underperforms CT-FM on TotalSegmentator variants, and underperforms Merlin substantially on Findings-to-image retrieval; the abstract/discussion framing is more triumphant than the results warrant.

No ablation isolating the contribution of individual architectural choices proposed as central contributions (windowed local+global attention design, RoPE jittering, anisotropic tokenization) against simpler baselines (e.g., plain 3D ViT, standard non-anisotropic patches) — the paper asserts these choices are necessary but provides no controlled comparison demonstrating their necessity versus the specific SSL/VLA recipe or larger data/compute budget being the actual driver of gains.

The comparisons across the 11 foundation models in Fig.1/Fig.3 and Tab.2/3 are not fully matched in training data, model size, or compute; it is unclear how much of SPECTRE's advantage stems from architectural novelty versus simply larger, more carefully curated pretraining data and far larger compute budget (24 B200 GPUs) than most baselines had access to, which confounds the paper's central architectural claims.

The paper does not report standard errors/uncertainty for the main Fig.1 radar comparison in the main text (only in supplementary Fig.3), and does not perform statistical significance testing for the '4/6 wins' claim, making it hard to assess whether the differences are meaningful versus noise for datasets with small sample sizes (e.g., 133-194 patients).

Some technical/architectural claims are asserted without ablation evidence in the main text, e.g., the omission of the DINOv3 Gram loss is justified qualitatively ('relatively narrow operational spectrum of the CT domain') without an experiment showing it would hurt or help.

The SEoMT segmentation results, while competitive, are consistently below the strongest baselines (nnU-Net ResEnc L, CT-FM) on several benchmarks, and the paper's own decoder ablation (Table 10) shows a substantially weaker detection rate for small lesions than nnU-Net ResEnc L, somewhat undermining the practical significance of segmentation results despite honest self-reporting.

The manuscript is dense and reads partly as a technical report; some notation (e.g., Eq. 15's D term, some symbol reuse) is imprecise or could be clarified, and heavy reliance on supplementary material makes the main paper less self-contained.

No comparison to very recent large multimodal 2D/3D medical foundation models beyond the specific chosen 11 baselines, and no discussion of computational cost/inference efficiency trade-offs of the two-stage local/global architecture versus simpler single-stage ViT baselines at equivalent parameter counts.

strengths: Trains exclusively on large-scale open CT data (229,619 series across 8 public datasets), addressing an important gap since many competing CT foundation models rely on private data; this improves reproducibility and community access.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct task families (biomarker classification via kNN on 6 datasets, semantic segmentation on 6+ benchmarks including KiTS23/LiTS/WORD/TotalSegmentator, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE/Merlin), compared against a wide set of 11 prior CT foundation models and multiple segmentation architectures.

Well-motivated architectural adaptations for volumetric CT (anisotropic 3D patch embedding matching typical CT voxel spacing ratios, two-stage local/global attention to make full-scan attention tractable, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style scale jittering) with clear complexity/engineering justification.

Thorough supplementary material: detailed dataset curation/filtering criteria, training hyperparameters, hardware specs, and multiple informative ablations (optimizer choice, crop size, decoder variants including a Linear vs SEoMT vs UNETR comparison with small-lesion detection-rate analysis).

Honest discussion of limitations (thoracic-heavy pretraining corpus, degraded performance on small lesions with the lightweight SEoMT decoder, noise in clinical reports) rather than overselling every result.

Practical VLA design choices addressing known 3D-specific issues, e.g., SigLIP loss to handle many-to-many image-report pairs and small effective batch sizes, and LLM-based report paraphrasing (LaCLIP-style) to combat report noise, with supporting robustness ablations (token/span dropout, report length).
weaknesses: The abstract's claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' is not fully supported: it wins on only 4/6 biomarker tasks (with wide, low-power confidence intervals on the 2 tasks it loses), is clearly beaten by CT-FM on TSv2-Full/TSv2-Merlin segmentation, and is substantially outperformed by Merlin on Findings-based retrieval (e.g., 55.5% vs 77.6% Recall@1 at N=32) despite the paper's framing implying broad superiority.

Segmentation gains over strong baselines are numerically small (e.g., 86.64% vs Primus-L's 86.04%, vs. nnU-Net ResEnc L's 88.06% on KiTS23) and no statistical significance test is reported, making it hard to assess whether the encoder actually provides a meaningful improvement over existing transformer backbones for this task.

The main paper presents no ablation isolating the individual contribution of the SSL (DINO) stage vs. the VLA (SigLIP) stage vs. the local/global two-stage attention design on the primary headline results (biomarker prediction, retrieval); most architectural justification is qualitative rather than empirically validated component-by-component.

Code/model release links are left blank in both the main text and supplementary ('Code available at:', GitHub link left empty), so reproducibility cannot currently be verified despite this being emphasized as a core contribution.

Pretraining requires an unusually large industrial compute budget (24 B200 GPUs across 3 DGX systems), which is not clearly discussed in terms of comparability/fairness to baselines trained with far less compute, and no compute-normalized comparison or efficiency benchmarking (throughput/memory vs. baselines) is provided despite 'efficient' being part of the architectural framing.

The SEoMT segmentation decoder is shown in the paper's own ablation (Table 10) to substantially underperform a more conventional UNETR-style decoder, especially on small lesions (detection rate 1.53% vs 11.12%), which somewhat undercuts the narrative that the encoder-only representation is a strong drop-in for dense prediction tasks without more decoder engineering.
